description_full: Winmark Corporation, a resale company, operates as a franchisor in the United States and Canada. It is involved in the operation of Plato's Closet, which franchisees buy and sell gently used clothing and accessories for the teenage and young adult market; Once Upon A Child, which franchisees buy and sell gently used and, to a lesser extent, new children's clothing, toys, furniture, equipment, and accessories; and Style Encore, which franchisees buy and sell gently used women's and men's apparel, shoes, and accessories. The company also operates Play It Again Sports, which franchisees buy, sell and trade gently used and new sporting goods, equipment, and accessories for various athletic activities, including team sports, fitness, ski and snowboard, and golf; Music Go Round, which franchisees buy, sell, and trade gently used and, to a lesser extent, new musical instruments, speakers, amplifiers, music-related electronics, and related accessories. In addition, it engages in the operation of a middle-market equipment leasing business under the Winmark Capital brand; and provision of point-of-sale system hardware to its franchisees and certain merchandise to its Play It Again Sports franchisees. The company was formerly known as Grow Biz International, Inc. and changed its name to Winmark Corporation in November 2001. Winmark Corporation was incorporated in 1988 and is headquartered in Minneapolis, Minnesota.

financial_summary: Winmark Corporation is a small-cap consumer cyclical business with a $967M market cap on $86M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +2% over the past three years and +2% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 87% against a 8% cost of capital — a 78-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $45M in free cash flow — roughly 52 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.08× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 22× is fortress-like.

Management returns a meaningful 5.3% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 17% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 8.0× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

Capex runs only 0.3x depreciation (0.2% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
own: Insiders own 17.3%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 88%.
